recipes.name: Maltese sweet pastry
recipes.summary: A lemon and orange scented sweet shortcrust for figolli, għadam tal-mejtin, sweet qassatat and Maltese tarts; one serving is the whole batch, about 590 g of dough.
method: Rub the cold, diced butter into the plain flour with your fingertips until it looks like fine crumbs.
Stir in the caster sugar, lemon zest and orange zest, then add the egg yolks and vanilla.
Work in the orange juice a little at a time until the dough just comes together; it should be soft but not sticky.
Press into a flat disc, wrap in cling film and chill for an hour before rolling.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Source for the traditional make-up: Apron & Whisk's figolli pastry (https://apronandwhisk.com/figolli-maltese-easter-treat/), with Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/6-local-treats-you-have-to-try-this-spring) for its use in figolli. One serving is one batch. Many Maltese bakers use margarine instead of butter; swap the line if you do. Freezes well, wrapped, for up to 3 months.

recipes.name: Maltese almond filling
recipes.summary: Ground almonds, caster sugar, egg white and lemon zest beaten to a soft paste with orange blossom water, for figolli and għadam tal-mejtin; one serving is half the batch, about 350 g.
method: Mix the ground almonds, caster sugar and lemon zest in a bowl.
Lightly beat the egg whites with a teaspoon of orange blossom water, then work them into the almonds a little at a time until you have a soft, spreadable paste.
Cover and chill for 30 minutes so it firms up before spreading.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Source for the traditional make-up: Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/6-local-treats-you-have-to-try-this-spring) for ground almonds, orange blossom water, lemon rind, egg white and caster sugar, and Apron & Whisk (https://apronandwhisk.com/figolli-maltese-easter-treat/) for the proportions. One serving is half the batch, enough for 6 figolli or 16 għadam tal-mejtin. Orange blossom water (ilma żahar) has no catalogue record and is left out of the lines; a teaspoon adds nothing measurable. Some bakers use icing sugar instead of caster sugar, or add almond essence.

recipes.name: Sweet ricotta filling
recipes.summary: Ricotta sweetened with icing sugar and vanilla, with chopped dark chocolate and candied peel, for zeppoli, sinizza, sweet qassatat and sweet ravjul; one serving is the whole batch, about 680 g.
method: Drain the ricotta in a sieve for 30 minutes if it is wet, then beat it smooth with the icing sugar and vanilla.
Chop the dark chocolate and candied peel finely and fold them in.
Cover and chill until needed; use within two days.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Source for the traditional make-up: Pippa Mattei's żeppoli filling in MaltaToday (https://www.maltatoday.com.mt/gourmet/recipes/85306/zeppoli_san_guzepp_recipe_pippa_mattei_malta_sfineg_ricotta) and Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/10-iconic-maltese-desserts-to-indulge-in). Fresh Maltese irkotta works best; swap the ricotta line for your Benna or Ħanini irkotta if you use it.

recipes.name: Chicken pastizzi
recipes.summary: Flaky pastry diamonds filled with chicken in a thick white sauce and baked until puffed. Makes 12; one serving is one pastizz.
method: Poach the chicken breast in gently simmering water for 15 to 18 minutes until cooked through, then cool and shred it very finely.
Melt the butter, soften the finely chopped onion in it for 5 minutes, stir in the flour, then whisk in the milk and simmer for 3 minutes into a very thick sauce.
Season with the nutmeg, salt and pepper, stir in the chicken and leave to cool completely; the filling must be thick and cold or the pastry will not seal.
Roll, cut and shape the puff pastry as for ricotta pastizzi, filling each of the 12 with a spoonful of the chicken mixture and pinching it into the diamond shape.
Bake at 200 °C for 25 to 30 minutes until puffed and golden.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Wiktionary and Wikipedia on the pastizz (https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/pastizz, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastizz) for chicken as a now-standard pastizzerija filling beside ricotta and pea, and a home recipe on gzrecipes (https://www.gzrecipes.com/en/ritaamordicucina/the-recipe-for-maltese-pastizzi/) for the creamy chicken, milk, flour and nutmeg filling. Pastizzeriji use their own laminated dough; this home version uses ready-made puff pastry like the ricotta and pea pastizzi. Some shops add peas or a little curry powder to the chicken; add them as lines if you do. The poaching water is thrown away, so it is not a line.

recipes.name: Easter almond pastries
recipes.summary: Sweet pastry shapes sandwiched with almond filling, baked, then iced and topped with a chocolate egg for Easter Sunday. Makes 6; one serving is one figolla.
method: Heat the oven to 180 °C and line a large tray. Roll out the sweet pastry about 5 mm thick and cut 12 matching shapes, such as lambs, fish or hearts, about 15 cm long.
Spread the almond filling over six of the shapes, leaving a 1 cm border; brush the border with water, cover with the matching shapes and press the edges to seal.
Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until lightly golden, then leave to cool completely, ideally overnight.
Whisk the egg white until foamy, then beat in the icing sugar and lemon juice until thick and glossy; spread it over the tops and pipe a border.
While the icing is soft, press half of one of the milk chocolate eggs onto each figolla if using, then leave to set for a few hours.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/6-local-treats-you-have-to-try-this-spring) for the ground almond, orange blossom water, lemon rind, egg white and caster sugar filling between two pastry shapes, the icing or chocolate finish and the half chocolate egg; Apron & Whisk (https://apronandwhisk.com/figolli-maltese-easter-treat/) for the pastry-to-filling proportions. Built from the Maltese sweet pastry and almond filling components. Many families coat them in melted chocolate instead of icing; swap the icing lines for chocolate if you do.

recipes.name: Gozitan cheeselet ftira with potato and egg
recipes.summary: A thin yeasted dough baked in a tray under sliced potato, fresh Gozo cheeselets and beaten egg.
method: Mix the bread flour, yeast, salt and water with a spoonful of the olive oil into a soft dough, knead for 8 minutes and leave to rise for about an hour.
Slice the potatoes paper-thin and toss them with most of the remaining olive oil and half the pepper.
Stretch the dough into a large oiled tray, letting it come a little way up the sides, and lay the potatoes over it in an even layer.

Crumble the fresh ġbejniet over the potatoes, beat the eggs with the chopped parsley and the rest of the pepper and pour them over; grate over the peppered ġbejna if using and drizzle with the last of the oil.
Bake at 220 °C for 30 to 35 minutes until the potatoes are tender, the egg is set and the base is crisp, then cut into 6.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Visit Gozo (https://visitgozo.com/2024/08/07/savouring-gozo-a-culinary-journey-through-mediterranean-flavours-and-traditional-dishes/) for fresh ġbejniet and beaten eggs over sliced potatoes, and Simon Bajada's Gozitan ftira on Clove (https://clove.kitchen/recipes/pizza-bread-gozo-ftira-ghawdxija-RCBdeSF7QEc) for the balance of eggs, fresh and peppered ġbejniet and potato. The cheeselet lines are Ħanini's fresh and peppered sheep's milk ġbejniet (one 300 g pack of fresh); swap in your own brand's label if it differs. Gozitan bakers use a sourdough dough; this home version uses dried yeast like the anchovy ftira. Some families add caramelised onion.

recipes.name: Carnival pine-nut cake
recipes.summary: A no-bake dome of crumbled sponge, crushed biscuits, roasted nuts and cherries bound with buttercream, covered in Italian meringue and finished with chocolate, glacé cherries and pine nuts. Cuts into 16.
method: Roast the pine nuts, hazelnuts and almonds at 180 °C for 6 to 8 minutes until golden; cool, keep 30 g of the pine nuts for the top and chop the rest roughly.
Beat the soft butter with the icing sugar until pale, then beat in the condensed milk and sweet vermouth to make a buttercream.

Crumble the orange sponge and crush the butter biscuits into a large bowl, add the chopped nuts, the candied peel and half the glacé cherries, chopped, then work in the buttercream with your hands until it holds together.
Pile onto a serving plate, shape into a tall dome, cover and chill overnight.

For the meringue, boil the sugar and water to 118 °C while you whisk the egg whites to soft peaks, then pour the hot syrup into the whites in a thin stream and whisk for 8 minutes until stiff and glossy.
Cover the dome with the meringue, drizzle with the melted dark chocolate and stud with the rest of the glacé cherries, halved, and the reserved pine nuts; slice into 16.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/malta-s-carnival-delight-some-facts-you-might-not-know-on-the-sweet-history-of-prinjolata) for sponge, biscuits, cream, condensed milk, vermouth, citrus peel, Italian meringue, chocolate, candied cherries and roasted pine nuts, and Apron & Whisk (https://apronandwhisk.com/prinjolata-maltese-carnival-dessert/) for the proportions. Uses 4 servings of the Gozitan orange sponge (pandispanja); about 200 g of any plain sponge will do. Petit Beurre or Morning Coffee biscuits are typical; the line uses a generic butter biscuit record. Sweet vermouth is counted with the catalogue's generic wine-based aperitif record; whisky or amaretto are common swaps.

recipes.name: St Joseph's ricotta fritters
recipes.summary: Choux fritters fried until hollow, filled with sweet ricotta and drizzled with Maltese honey and roasted almonds for St Joseph's Day, 19 March. Makes 14; one serving is one fritter.
method: Bring the water, butter and salt to the boil, tip in the plain flour all at once and beat over a low heat for a minute or two until the dough leaves the sides of the pan.
Cool for 5 minutes, then beat in the eggs one at a time with the orange zest and lemon zest until smooth and glossy.
Heat the sunflower oil to 170 °C and fry spoonfuls of the dough a few at a time for 6 to 8 minutes, turning, until puffed, deep golden and hollow; drain and cool.
Split each fritter and pipe or spoon in the sweet ricotta filling.
Drizzle with the honey, scatter with the chopped roasted almonds and eat within the hour, before the pastry softens.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/10-iconic-maltese-desserts-to-indulge-in) for fried dough balls with sweet ricotta and Maltese honey for 19 March; Pippa Mattei in MaltaToday (https://www.maltatoday.com.mt/gourmet/recipes/85306/zeppoli_san_guzepp_recipe_pippa_mattei_malta_sfineg_ricotta) for the choux and filling proportions; Tisjir (https://www.tisjir.com/sfineg/) for the roasted almond finish. The frying oil line (60 g) is an estimate of what 14 fritters absorb, not the oil in the pan. Some bakeries fill them with custard or pastry cream instead.

recipes.name: Honey fritters
recipes.summary: Flat pieces of soft yeast dough fried until puffed and crisp, then turned in warm honey. Makes 12; one serving is one fritter.
method: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt, then add the warm water and olive oil and knead into a soft dough; cover and leave to rise for about an hour until doubled.
Divide into 12 pieces and, with oiled hands, stretch each into a flat round about the size of your palm.
Fry a few at a time in hot sunflower oil for 2 to 3 minutes a side until puffed and golden; drain on kitchen paper.
Warm the honey in a small pan until runny, turn each hot fritter in it to coat and serve with tea or coffee.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/6-local-treats-you-have-to-try-this-spring) for flat pieces of bread dough fried and coated in honey, eaten with tea or coffee; Apron & Whisk's sfineġ (https://apronandwhisk.com/sfineg-tal-incova-traditional-maltese-anchovy-fritters/) for the flour, yeast and water dough. The frying oil line (50 g) is an estimate of what 12 fritters absorb, and the honey line assumes most of it clings.

recipes.name: Apostles' bread ring
recipes.summary: A slightly sweet olive-oil bread ring for Holy Week, topped with sesame, twelve whole almonds for the apostles and candied peel. Cuts into 10.
method: Mix the lukewarm water, yeast and sugar and leave for 10 to 15 minutes until frothy.
Mix the bread flour and salt, add the olive oil and the yeast mixture and knead for 10 minutes into a soft, slightly sticky dough; cover and leave to rise for about an hour until doubled.
Knock back, roll into a rope about 60 cm long and join the ends into a ring on a lined tray.
Brush with water, scatter over the sesame seeds, press in the 12 whole almonds and the candied peel, and leave to rise for 45 minutes while the oven heats to 200 °C.
Bake for 35 to 40 minutes until deep golden and hollow-sounding underneath; cool before cutting into 10, and eat plain or toasted with butter.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Visit Gozo (https://visitgozo.com/2024/10/22/delectable-treats-more-gozos-sweets-indulgences/) for a slightly sweet Holy Week ring topped with candied peel and almonds; Apron & Whisk (https://apronandwhisk.com/qaghqa-tal-appostli-maltese-apostles-ring-bread/) for the olive-oil dough, sesame and the twelve almonds; Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/ash-wednesday-is-upon-us---here-are-seven-traditional-maltese-treats-to-eat-this-lent) for eating it plain or toasted. Sweetness varies a lot; some bakers use only a teaspoon of sugar. Butter for toasting is not included.

recipes.name: Sweet aniseed yeast rings
recipes.summary: Small soft rings of sweet milk dough scented with aniseed, cloves and orange zest and topped with sesame. Makes 18; one serving is one ring.
method: Warm the milk and water to blood heat, stir in the yeast and sugar and leave for 10 to 15 minutes until frothy.

Mix the bread flour, aniseed, cloves and orange zest, add the soft margarine and the yeast mixture and knead for 10 minutes into a soft, sticky dough; cover and leave to rise for an hour until doubled.
Divide into 18 pieces, roll each into a rope about 20 cm long and join the ends into a ring.
Dip the top of each ring in the sesame seeds, set them on a lined tray and leave to rise for 30 minutes while the oven heats to 220 °C.
Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until golden, and eat warm or cold, plain or dunked in tea.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes) for a soft, sweet ring with a hint of aniseed topped with sesame; Apron & Whisk (https://apronandwhisk.com/qaghaq-tal-hmira-maltese-yeast-rings/) for the milk dough, cloves, orange zest and margarine. Some recipes use butter and lemon zest instead.

recipes.name: Maltese ricotta puff roll
recipes.summary: Puff pastry brushed with honey, rose water and nutmeg, wrapped around orange sponge, jam and sweet ricotta with candied peel, topped with almonds and honey and baked. Cuts into 12.
method: Heat the oven to 200 °C. Warm the honey with the nutmeg and a teaspoon of rose water, and unroll the puff pastry onto a lined tray.
Brush the pastry with a little of the spiced honey, then lay slices of the orange sponge down the middle, sprinkle them with the sweet vermouth and spread with the jam.
Spoon the sweet ricotta filling over the sponge, fold the pastry over to enclose it in a long oval roll, pinch the seam and turn it seam-side down.
Brush with the beaten egg, scatter over the flaked almonds and pour the rest of the spiced honey over the top.
Bake for 30 to 35 minutes until puffed and deep golden, then cool completely before cutting into 12.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/10-iconic-maltese-desserts-to-indulge-in) for the rose water, nutmeg and honey pastry, the ricotta and candied peel filling and the nuts and honey poured on before baking; Visit Gozo (https://visitgozo.com/2024/10/22/delectable-treats-more-gozos-sweets-indulgences/) for sponge, jam, ricotta, liqueur, candied peel, nuts and chocolate; Simon Bajada's sinizza on Great British Chefs (https://www.greatbritishchefs.com/recipes/sinizza-recipe) for proportions. Rose water has no catalogue record and is left out of the lines; a teaspoon adds nothing measurable. Confectioners make their own rose-water pastry; this home version flavours shop puff pastry with the honey glaze. Sweet vermouth is counted with the catalogue's generic wine-based aperitif record.

recipes.name: Maltese almond tart
recipes.summary: A sweet pastry case filled with ground almonds, honey, orange rind and egg white under a pastry lattice, made for festas and weddings. Cuts into 12.
method: Heat the oven to 180 °C. Roll out two-thirds of the sweet pastry, line a 23 cm tart tin and chill it while you make the filling.
Mix the ground almonds, caster sugar, honey, orange rind, lemon rind and vanilla, then work in the egg whites to make a soft, thick paste.
Spread the filling in the pastry case and level it.
Roll out the rest of the pastry, cut it into strips and lay them over the filling as a lattice; scatter the flaked almonds in the gaps.
Bake for 35 to 40 minutes until the pastry is golden and the filling is set; cool in the tin before cutting into 12.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/10-iconic-maltese-desserts-to-indulge-in) for a pastry-covered almond, honey and orange rind filling made for festas and weddings; Benna's almond tart (https://www.benna.com.mt/recipes/almond-tart/) for the ground almond, egg white, honey and citrus zest filling. Most recipes add almond essence, which has no catalogue record and is left out; the amount is too small to change the totals much.

recipes.name: Almond and chocolate tart
recipes.summary: A sweet pastry case filled with almonds, crushed rusks, candied peel, cocoa, orange and sweet spice, covered in a dark chocolate fudge frosting marbled with white icing. Cuts into 10.
method: Heat the oven to 190 °C. Roll out the sweet pastry and line a 23 cm tart tin.
Crush the rusks finely and mix them with the ground almonds, chopped candied peel, marmalade, egg, caster sugar, orange juice, cocoa, cinnamon and cloves into a thick, moist filling.
Spread the filling in the case and bake for 25 to 30 minutes until the pastry is golden and the filling firm; leave to cool.
Melt the dark chocolate with the frosting sugar, milk and butter, stirring until smooth, and pour it over the cooled tart.
Mix the icing sugar with the lemon juice to a thick icing, pipe thin lines across the soft chocolate and drag a skewer through them to marble; leave to set before cutting into 10.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/10-iconic-maltese-desserts-to-indulge-in) for an almond and sweet spice filling topped with dark chocolate and icing; Tal-Forn (https://www.tal-forn.com/2013/08/torta-tal-marmurat-almond-and-chocolate-tart/) for the rusks, candied peel, marmalade, cocoa, orange juice and the chocolate fudge frosting. It is rarely sold in bakeries and family recipes vary a lot; some add ricotta or tangerine marmalade.

recipes.name: All Souls' almond bone pastries
recipes.summary: Bone-shaped sweet pastries sandwiched with almond filling and covered in white icing, made in November for All Souls' Day. Makes 16; one serving is one bone.
method: Heat the oven to 180 °C and line two trays. Roll out the sweet pastry about 4 mm thick and cut 32 bone shapes about 12 cm long.
Mix the cloves into the almond filling if using, then spread it over 16 of the bones, leaving a small border; brush the edges with water, cover with the remaining bones and press to seal.
Bake for 20 to 25 minutes until pale golden, then cool completely.
Whisk the egg white until foamy, beat in the icing sugar and lemon juice until thick and glossy, and spread it over the tops; leave to set.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Wikipedia, Maltese cuisine (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maltese_cuisine) for a layer of marzipan between sweet pastry topped with white icing, made in November; KM Malta Airlines (https://kmmaltairlines.com/en/blog/latest/dead-men-s-bones) for the ground almond, sugar, egg white and lemon rind filling; Oh My Malta (https://issuu.com/ohmymalta/docs/oh_my_malta_november_2022/s/17261136) for the optional spice and the likeness to figolli. Built from the same sweet pastry and almond filling as figolli; only the shape differs.

recipes.name: Lenten honey pastry squares
recipes.summary: A plain flour and water dough rolled very thin, cut into squares, deep-fried until crisp and drizzled with honey. Makes 24 squares; one serving is two.
method: Mix the flour and salt, add the water a little at a time and knead for 5 minutes into a smooth, firm dough; cover and rest for 30 minutes.
Divide into 6 balls, roll each out as thinly as you can and cut each sheet into 4 squares.
Deep-fry a few at a time in hot sunflower oil for about a minute a side until blistered, crisp and pale golden; drain on kitchen paper.
Warm the honey until runny and drizzle it over the squares while they are still warm.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes) for Lenten honey-drizzled squares of crisp deep-fried pastry, and a Lenten bread recipe titled Ftira tar-Randan on Food.com (https://www.food.com/recipe/lenten-bread-ftira-tar-randan-424622) for the plain three-ingredient dough rested, rolled thin and fried. Neither gives exact quantities, so treat the proportions as a home version. The frying oil line (50 g) is an estimate of what the squares absorb.

recipes.name: St Martin's sweet bun
recipes.summary: Soft sweet milk buns scented with aniseed and vanilla, glazed with sugar syrup and sesame, made for St Martin's Day on 11 November. Makes 8; one serving is one bun.
method: Warm the milk to blood heat, stir in the yeast and a spoonful of the sugar and leave for 15 minutes until frothy.

Rub the butter into the bread flour, add the rest of the sugar, the aniseed, vanilla and salt, then the yeast mixture, and knead for 10 to 15 minutes into a soft dough; cover and leave to rise for an hour until doubled.
Knock back, divide into 8 balls and set them well apart on a lined tray; leave to rise for 20 minutes while the oven heats to 200 °C.
Dissolve the glaze sugar in the water, brush it over the buns and scatter with the sesame seeds.
Bake for about 15 minutes until golden, and press one of the liquorice sweets into the top of each hot bun if using.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes) for a sweet bread roll flavoured with mastic for St Martin's Day; Apron & Whisk (https://apronandwhisk.com/wprm_print/hobza-ta-san-martin-st-martins-sweet-bun) for the milk dough with aniseed and vanilla, the sugar glaze, sesame and the liquorice sweet on top. Mastic (mastika) has no catalogue record; add a pinch, ground with a little of the sugar, with the aniseed if you have it, as it adds nothing measurable. The bun traditionally goes in the borża ta' San Martin, a bag of nuts and fruit. The liquorice line uses a generic liquorice allsorts record.

recipes.name: Traditional Maltese ice cream
recipes.summary: A no-churn ice cream of evaporated and condensed milk with cinnamon and lemon, whipped with cream and studded with roasted almonds and candied peel. Serves 10.
method: Whisk the evaporated milk, condensed milk, cinnamon, lemon zest and vanilla together, pour into a freezer container and freeze for 3 to 4 hours until slushy and frozen at the edges.
Whip the whipping cream to soft peaks, and chop the roasted almonds, the candied peel and the glacé cherries if using.
Tip the half-frozen mixture into a bowl and beat with an electric whisk for 5 minutes until pale and nearly doubled.
Fold in the cream, almonds, peel and cherries, return to the container, scatter a few of the almonds on top and freeze overnight.
Soften in the fridge for 15 minutes before scooping.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes) for condensed milk, cinnamon, nuts and candied peel; Taste Valletta (https://taste-valletta.com/hello-world/) for condensed milk, cream, roasted almonds, candied peel, cinnamon, lemon and vanilla; Anna Sultana's Maltese ice cream (https://imturning60help.blogspot.com/2016/07/anna-sultanas-gelatt-ice-cream-maltese.html) for the evaporated milk base. Many families use only evaporated milk, boiled with sugar, a cinnamon stick and lemon rind; others add chocolate chips.

recipes.name: Gozitan orange sponge cake
recipes.summary: A light, fatless whisked sponge flavoured with orange or tangerine zest and juice, eaten plain or used as the base for trifle, prinjolata, sinizza and semifreddo. Cuts into 10.
method: Heat the oven to 180 °C and grease and line a 23 cm round tin.
Whisk the eggs and caster sugar with an electric whisk for 8 to 10 minutes until very pale and thick enough to leave a ribbon.
Briefly whisk in the orange zest and orange juice, then sift over the plain flour in three goes, folding it in gently so you keep the air.
Pour into the tin and bake for 30 to 35 minutes until golden and springy; cool on a rack and dust with the icing sugar if serving it plain.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Visit Gozo (https://visitgozo.com/2024/10/22/delectable-treats-more-gozos-sweets-indulgences/) for the Gozitan sponge flavoured with oranges or tangerines and used as the base for trifle; the whisked-egg method as in Simon Bajada's sinizza sponge on Great British Chefs (https://www.greatbritishchefs.com/recipes/sinizza-recipe). Use the zest and juice of two tangerines instead of the orange if you have them. Other recipes use it by the serving: 4 to 6 servings is roughly half the cake.

recipes.name: Maltese trifle
recipes.summary: Orange sponge soaked in sweet vermouth under strawberry jelly, a thick layer of custard and whipped cream, finished with glacé cherries and almonds. Serves 10.
method: Make up the strawberry jelly from its packet with boiling water and leave it to cool until syrupy but not set.
Cut the orange sponge into fingers and pack them into the bottom of a large glass bowl; sprinkle with the sweet vermouth and scatter over the drained fruit cocktail if using.
Pour the jelly over the sponge and chill for about 2 hours until set.

Mix the custard powder and sugar to a paste with a little of the milk, heat the rest of the milk, stir in the paste and cook, stirring, until thick; cover the surface and cool, then spread over the set jelly.
Whip the whipping cream with the icing sugar to soft peaks and spread it over the custard; decorate with the glacé cherries and chopped roasted almonds and chill for an hour before serving.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Visit Gozo (https://visitgozo.com/2024/10/22/delectable-treats-more-gozos-sweets-indulgences/) for sponge cake under custard, jelly, whipped cream and a generous splash of vermouth; a Maltese trifle on World Nomads (https://journals.worldnomads.com/joni/photos/53085/Malta/Passport-and-Plate-Maltese-Trifle) for custard made from custard powder and the cherry and almond finish. The jelly line is one packet, counted as made-up jelly. Sweet vermouth is counted with the catalogue's generic wine-based aperitif record. The fruit cocktail line is one 420 g tin in light syrup, drained (about 240 g), using the generic Ciqual record; Mayor's tin is the usual Maltese one. Not vegetarian: packet jelly is set with gelatine.

recipes.name: Pink coconut cakes
recipes.summary: Squares of butter sponge dipped in pink strawberry jelly and rolled in desiccated coconut, a Maltese bakery staple. Makes 15; one serving is one cake.
method: Heat the oven to 180 °C and line a 20 cm square tin. Beat the soft butter and sugar until pale, then beat in the eggs and vanilla.
Fold in the self-raising flour and salt, then the milk; spread in the tin and bake for 20 to 25 minutes until springy, and cool completely, ideally overnight.
Dissolve a packet of strawberry jelly crystals in 200 ml boiling water and leave until cool and just starting to thicken.
Cut the sponge into 15 squares, dip each one in the strawberry jelly to coat it all over, then roll it in the desiccated coconut and set on a tray until firm.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Visit Gozo (https://visitgozo.com/2024/10/22/delectable-treats-more-gozos-sweets-indulgences/) for pink and coconut cakes in Maltese bakeries; KM Malta Airlines (https://kmmaltairlines.com/en/blog/latest/fancy-a-bambaluna) for the pink lamington, called pasta roża or, in Gozo, bambaluna; Apron & Whisk's pasta roża (https://apronandwhisk.com/wprm_print/pink-lamingtons-pasta-mir-roza) for the butter sponge and the jelly and coconut coating. The jelly line counts three-quarters of one packet, as made-up jelly, since some is left in the bowl; the coconut line is what clings, not the whole bag. Not vegetarian: packet jelly is set with gelatine.

recipes.name: Iced sweet pastry biscuits
recipes.summary: Long fingers of Maltese sweet pastry baked crisp and covered in pink icing, or striped pink and green. Makes 24; one serving is one biscuit.
method: Heat the oven to 180 °C and line two trays. Roll out the sweet pastry about 5 mm thick and cut it into 24 fingers about 9 by 3 cm.
Bake for 12 to 15 minutes until pale golden at the edges, then cool on a rack.
Mix the icing sugar with the lemon juice and enough of the water to make a thick, spreadable icing, and tint it pink with a drop of food colouring, or split it and tint half green.
Spread the pink icing over each biscuit, or pipe alternate pink and green stripes, and leave to set.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Source for the traditional make-up: Visit Gozo (https://visitgozo.com/2024/10/22/delectable-treats-more-gozos-sweets-indulgences/) for long sweet pastry biscuits fully covered in pink icing or decorated with pink and green stripes; the pastry is the Maltese sweet pastry component. Food colouring is left out of the lines; a drop adds nothing measurable.

recipes.name: Village biscuits with icing swirls
recipes.summary: Soft, crumbly round biscuits spiced with caraway, aniseed, cinnamon and cloves, each topped with a swirl of pink or pale blue icing. Makes 30; one serving is one biscuit.
method: Heat the oven to 180 °C and line two trays. Cream the butter with the sugar and brown sugar until fluffy, then beat in the eggs and vanilla.
Crush the caraway seeds and aniseed, mix them with the plain flour, baking powder, cinnamon, cloves and salt, and work into the butter mixture to a soft, slightly sticky dough.
Roll into 30 balls, space them out on the trays and bake for about 18 minutes until lightly golden; cool on a rack.
Whisk the egg white until foamy, beat in the icing sugar and lemon juice until thick and glossy, and tint it pink or pale blue with a drop of food colouring.
Pipe a swirl of icing on top of each biscuit and leave to dry completely.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Visit Gozo (https://visitgozo.com/2024/10/22/delectable-treats-more-gozos-sweets-indulgences/) for the swirl of light blue or pink icing; Apron & Whisk (https://apronandwhisk.com/biskuttini-tar-rahal/) for the caraway, aniseed, cinnamon and clove biscuit; the Maltese christening biscuit on Food.com (https://www.food.com/recipe/christening-biscuit-maltese-297521) for the pink or blue swirl. Written as its own base rather than a variant of biskuttini tal-lewż: Visit Gozo likens them to almond macaroons, but the only full Maltese recipe found makes a spiced flour biscuit with no almonds. Food colouring is left out of the lines; a drop adds nothing measurable.

recipes.name: Date and cocoa tart
recipes.summary: A sweet pastry case filled with dates cooked down with cocoa, orange, aniseed and cloves, enriched with walnuts and egg, under a pastry lattice. Cuts into 12.
method: Chop the dates and simmer them with the water, orange juice, orange zest, cocoa, sugar, aniseed and cloves for 10 to 15 minutes, mashing, until thick and jammy; leave to cool.
Heat the oven to 180 °C. Roll out two-thirds of the sweet pastry and line a 23 cm tart tin.
Beat the egg into the cooled date mixture, stir in the chopped walnuts and spread the filling in the case.
Cut the rest of the pastry into strips, lay them over the filling as a lattice and bake for 35 to 40 minutes until golden; cool before cutting into 12.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes) for a date and cocoa tart; Oh My Malta (https://issuu.com/ohmymalta/docs/oh_my_malta_august_2022/37) naming date pie as torta tat-tamal; Saveur's Maltese-style cocoa date pie (https://www.saveur.com/article/Recipes/Cocoa-Date-Pie) for the cocoa, orange, walnut, anise and egg filling. Saveur uses sambuca; it has no catalogue record, so aniseed is used instead, as in imqaret.

recipes.name: Sweet fried ricotta ravioli
recipes.summary: Small ravjul of thin, lightly sweetened pasta filled with sweet ricotta, deep-fried until crisp and rolled in cinnamon sugar. Makes 30; one serving is three.
method: Mix the flour, semolina and sugar, add the eggs and water and knead for 8 minutes into a firm, smooth dough; wrap and rest for 30 minutes.

Roll the dough out very thinly into two sheets, put teaspoons of the sweet ricotta filling in rows on one sheet, cover with the other and press around each mound; cut out 30 ravjul and seal the edges well.
Deep-fry a few at a time in hot sunflower oil for 2 to 3 minutes until golden and crisp; drain on kitchen paper.
Mix the coating sugar with the cinnamon and roll the hot ravjul in it; serve warm.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes) for sweet toasted ravioli; Aceline Media, a Gozo-based publisher (https://aceline.media/recipes/sweet-fried-ricotta-ravioli-with-orange-hot-chocolate-sauce/), for ricotta ravjul deep-fried and rolled in cinnamon sugar; the flour and semolina dough as in Maltese ravjul. Neither source gives a traditional filling formula, so this uses the sweet ricotta filling; treat the proportions as a home version. The frying oil line (60 g) is an estimate of what 30 ravjul absorb.

recipes.name: Sweet ricotta qassatat
recipes.summary: Open sweet-pastry cups gathered around sweetened ricotta with chocolate and candied peel, each topped with a glacé cherry; an Easter-season sweet. Makes 8; one serving is one.
method: Heat the oven to 190 °C and line a tray. Beat the egg into the sweet ricotta filling.
Roll out the sweet pastry and cut 8 rounds of about 13 cm; pile the filling in the centre of each and gather the edges up around it in pleats, leaving the top open.
Press one of the glacé cherries into the middle of each and bake for 25 to 30 minutes until the pastry is golden and the filling is set.
Cool, and dust with the icing sugar if you like.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Horeca Malta (https://horecamalta.com.mt/2025/04/11/past-meets-pastry-the-evolution-of-easters-sweetest-traditions/) for the Easter-season sweet twist on the savoury qassata; Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/ash-wednesday-is-upon-us---here-are-seven-traditional-maltese-treats-to-eat-this-lent) for a sweet tart with a sugary ricotta filling topped with a cherry; Lolly's Kitchen (https://lollyskitchen.com.mt/?p=13149) for sweet shortcrust around ricotta with chocolate and nuts. Some bakers add chopped roasted almonds or cinnamon to the filling.

recipes.name: Maltese Christmas log
recipes.summary: A no-bake log of crushed biscuits, cocoa, roasted nuts, glacé cherries and candied peel bound with condensed milk and a splash of vermouth, coated in dark chocolate bark. Cuts into 16.
method: Roast the walnuts, hazelnuts and almonds at 180 °C for 8 minutes, then cool and chop roughly.
Crush the butter biscuits finely and mix them with the cocoa, the nuts, the glacé cherries, halved, and the candied peel.
Add the condensed milk, and the sweet vermouth if using, and work everything together with your hands into a sticky dough.
Shape into a log about 30 cm long on baking paper, spread with the melted dark chocolate and drag a fork along it so it looks like bark.
Leave in a cool place, not the fridge, until the chocolate sets, then dust with the icing sugar and cut into 16 slices.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Sources for the traditional make-up: Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/yummy-these-are-malta-s-5-favourite-christmas-treats) for a log of biscuits, dried fruit and nuts instead of sponge; Apron & Whisk (https://apronandwhisk.com/maltese-christmas-log/) for the proportions, condensed milk, cocoa, optional vermouth and chocolate bark; KM Malta Airlines (https://kmmaltairlines.com/en/blog/latest/maltas-beloved-christmas-log) for the mix of walnuts, hazelnuts and almonds. The Maltese name is a working label. Families swap the vermouth for whisky or brandy, or add chocolate chips. Morning Coffee or Petit Beurre biscuits are typical; the line uses a generic butter biscuit record, and the vermouth a generic wine-based aperitif record.

recipes.name: Maltese semifreddo
recipes.summary: A frozen loaf of vermouth-soaked orange sponge around vanilla ice cream folded with whipped cream, candied fruit, chocolate and pistachios. Cuts into 10.
method: Line a 900 g loaf tin with cling film. Cut the orange sponge into thin slices, line the base and sides of the tin with about two-thirds of them and sprinkle with the sweet vermouth.
Soften the vanilla ice cream in the fridge for 15 minutes, and whip the whipping cream with the icing sugar to soft peaks.
Chop the candied peel, glacé cherries, dark chocolate and pistachios and fold them, with the cream, into the softened ice cream.
Spoon into the lined tin, level, cover with the rest of the sponge slices and freeze for at least 6 hours.
Turn out, peel off the film and cut into 10 slices with a hot knife.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Source for the traditional make-up: Visit Malta (https://www.visitmalta.com/fr/food-and-drink), which names Sicilian-style semifreddo, a mix of sponge, ice cream, candied fruit and cream, among Malta's favourite desserts. No Maltese source gives proportions, so treat them as a home version; confectioners' versions vary and some use a ricotta or custard base instead of ice cream. Sweet vermouth is counted with the catalogue's generic wine-based aperitif record.
